items.text: When the innocent suffer, someone must be held responsible for it.
items.evidence: After Neil's death the demand that someone answer for it produces the scapegoating of Keating rather than justice.

items.text: Those who yield to coercion against their conscience deserve forgiveness rather than condemnation.
items.evidence: 'Todd reluctantly signs under his parents' pressure'... 'Keating assures Todd that he believes him' — the coerced boy is forgiven, not condemned.

items.text: Wrongdoing is properly traced to a single guilty party who can be identified and punished.
items.evidence: Keating is made the single culpable party and fired, a resolution the film presents as an injustice.

items.text: Institutions that have endured and produced results have earned deference in how they shape the young.
items.evidence: Welton's 'strict headmaster' paddles Charlie, coerces signatures on 'false allegations', and fires Keating; the institution's discipline is shown as corrupt rather than earned deference.

items.text: Institutions of learning and governance can themselves be instruments of oppression rather than safeguards against it.
items.evidence: Nolan paddles a student to extract names, threatens expulsion for anyone who 'speaks out of line', and scapegoats Keating after Neil's death.

items.text: There is a correct method for evaluating works of art, one that can be taught and applied.
items.evidence: Keating 'tells them to rip out the introduction of their poetry books that explains a mathematical formula for rating poetry'.

items.text: Silence in the face of unjust power is a betrayal even when the pressure to stay silent is overwhelming.
items.evidence: 'Todd confesses that the boys were pressured into signing the letter'; he then stands on his desk despite Nolan's expulsion threat, and the film treats this as its triumph.

items.text: A person should hold to a moral conviction even when every institution, friend and loved one urges compromise.
items.evidence: Charlie 'refuses' to name the club members under paddling and is expelled for punching Cameron; Todd defies Nolan's threat.

items.text: Official institutions reliably discover the truth of what has happened and assign responsibility justly.
items.evidence: 'Nolan investigates his death' but the inquiry produces 'false allegations' against Keating and coerced signatures.

items.text: Courage requires prudence: reckless defiance is not the same as bravery.
items.evidence: 'Keating gently admonishes him, advising the boys that one must assess all potential consequences of one's actions' after Charlie's newspaper stunt.

items.text: To witness wrongdoing and do nothing is itself a moral position, one a person must eventually abandon.
items.evidence: Todd signs the letter under pressure but finally speaks and stands, and the other boys follow — the abandonment of silence is the validated ending.

items.text: Private conscience is a higher court than either the law or the claims of one's family.
items.evidence: Todd defies both his parents' pressure and Nolan's threat of expulsion in order to affirm the truth about Keating.

items.text: Habitually waiting for permission instead of acting on one's own judgment is a defect of character that a person ought to outgrow.
items.evidence: Todd, the shy boy who signs under pressure, is brought out of his shell and finally acts on his own judgment by standing on the desk.

items.text: Authority earns obedience by how it conducts itself rather than by the office it holds.
items.evidence: Nolan holds the office but commands only fear; Keating, stripped of his post, still commands the boys' allegiance.

items.text: An inner transformation that changes nothing about the world's arrangements is nonetheless a real and sufficient victory.
items.evidence: Keating still departs and Nolan still rules the school, yet the boys' standing on their desks is staged as the film's victorious close: 'Touched by their support, Keating proudly thanks the boys and departs.'

items.text: Being able to put one's inner experience into words is what wins a person their chance in life.
items.evidence: Todd's exercise 'in self-expression' produces a poem that releases him, while Neil, 'unable to explain his feelings to his father', dies.

items.text: A person's first duty is to discover and express what is genuinely inside them, rather than to fulfil the role assigned by family and institution.
items.evidence: Keating's classes teach the boys to 'look at life differently' and 'form their individualism'; Neil discovers his love of acting against his father's plan for medical school, and Todd's spontaneous poem is presented as a breakthrough.

items.text: A person's own calling should take precedence over the role their family and community have assigned them.
items.evidence: Neil 'discovers his love of acting and wins the role of Puck... despite the disapproval of his authoritarian father, who wants him to attend medical school'; the father's imposition ends in tragedy.

items.text: Children owe obedience to their parents' direction of their lives until they become independent.
items.evidence: Neil's father 'demands that he quit' and plans to enroll him in military school; 'a devastated Neil commits suicide' — the film frames paternal direction as destructive.

items.text: A parent's authority over the direction of a child's life is rightly final.
items.evidence: The 'authoritarian father' who overrides Neil's calling precipitates his suicide; Todd's signing 'under his parents' pressure' is presented as coerced wrongdoing.

items.text: A teacher's proper task is to hand on a body of knowledge and discipline, not to awaken a pupil's individual sensibility.
items.evidence: Keating, the film's moral centre, has students rip out the poetry-rating formula and invent their own walks; Nolan's takeover of the class is presented as loss.

items.text: Awareness that life is short is the proper foundation of how a person should act.
items.evidence: 'Keating teaches them the Latin expression carpe diem, encouraging them to "seize the day"' — the organizing precept of the film.

items.text: Conformity to the group is a danger to be resisted, even at cost to one's standing.
items.evidence: The courtyard walking exercise 'to form their individualism'; the closing desk-standing occurs 'despite the threat' of expulsion.

items.text: Every person is entitled to a life of their own, separate from the claims of family.
items.evidence: Neil's inability to claim a life apart from his father's plan for Harvard Medical School is the film's central catastrophe.

items.text: Beauty, art and love are not ornaments to a useful life but the reason for living at all.
items.evidence: Poetry, the secret club readings, and Neil's acting are set against the utilitarian path of medical school as what makes life worth living.

items.text: Obedience to elders is the primary virtue of the young.
items.evidence: Obedience to Nolan and to Neil's father is what produces the film's disasters; the boys' defiance is rewarded by the ending.

items.text: A life spent in resigned acceptance of one's circumstances is a life wasted.
items.evidence: 'Keating's lessons and the conversations in the club encourage them to live on their own terms', against passive acceptance of Welton's prescribed path.

items.text: Wisdom cannot be received by being told; it must be arrived at through one's own experience.
items.evidence: Keating has students 'take turns standing on his desk to demonstrate ways to look at life differently' rather than instructing them by lecture.

items.text: A person whose desires fall outside what their community permits should be accepted as they are rather than corrected.
items.evidence: Neil's acting is punished with withdrawal to Braden Military School rather than accepted, and the film treats that correction as fatal.

items.text: Vows and confidences create real obligations, and betraying them is the paradigmatic wrong.
items.evidence: 'Cameron shifts blame onto Keating to avoid punishment... and he names the other members. Charlie punches him for his betrayal.'

items.text: Doing what is right carries real costs that its goodness does not cancel, and the innocent still suffer.
items.evidence: Charlie's refusal costs him expulsion, Neil's self-assertion ends in his death, and Keating loses his post despite being right.

items.text: Persistent effort and moral determination are eventually rewarded with a just outcome.
items.evidence: Neil dies, Charlie is expelled, Keating is fired and Nolan takes over the class — moral courage brings no just outcome.

items.text: What one person plants in another survives the death of the one who planted it.
items.evidence: After Keating's dismissal the boys stand and call 'O Captain! My Captain!' — what he planted persists past his removal.

## Plot
In the fall of 1959, Todd Anderson begins his junior year of high school at Welton Academy, an Episcopal all-male preparatory boarding school in Vermont. He is assigned one of Welton's top students, Neil Perry, as his roommate, and meets Neil's friends: Knox Overstreet, Richard Cameron, Steven Meeks, Gerard Pitts, and Charlie Dalton.
On the first day of classes, the boys meet their new English teacher, John Keating, a Welton alumnus who studied English literature at the University of Cambridge. Keating teaches them the Latin expression carpe diem, encouraging them to "seize the day". During his classes, he has the students take turns standing on his desk to demonstrate ways to look at life differently, tells them to rip out the introduction of their poetry books that explains a mathematical formula for rating poetry, and invites them to make up their own style of walking in a courtyard to form their individualism. These unusual methods attract the attention of strict headmaster, Gale Nolan.
Upon learning that Keating had been a member of the unofficial Dead Poets Society during his time as a student, Neil restarts the club. He and his friends sneak off campus to a cave to read poetry. Keating's lessons and the conversations in the club encourage them to live on their own terms.
Knox pursues Chris Noel, a cheerleader who is dating Chet Danburry, a football player whose family is friends with his. Neil discovers his love of acting and wins the role of Puck in a local production of A Midsummer Night's Dream despite the disapproval of his authoritarian father, who wants him to attend medical school. Keating helps Todd come out of his shell when he takes him through an exercise in self-expression, resulting in his spontaneous composition of a poem in front of the class.
Charlie publishes an article in the school newspaper on behalf of the Dead Poets Society recommending that girls be admitted to Welton. In response, Nolan paddles Charlie, attempting to force him to reveal the names of the other members of the Dead Poets Society; Charlie refuses. Keating gently admonishes him, advising the boys that one must assess all potential consequences of one's actions.
On the eve of the play's opening performance, Neil's father discovers his involvement and demands that he quit. Neil performs in the play, but his father retaliates by telling him he plans to withdraw him from Welton and enroll him in Braden Military School in preparation for Harvard Medical School. Lacking support from his mother and unable to explain his feelings to his father, a devastated Neil commits suicide.
At Neil's parents' request, Nolan investigates his death. Cameron shifts blame onto Keating to avoid punishment for his role in the Dead Poets Society, and he names the other members of the group. Charlie punches him for his betrayal and is expelled. Each of the boys is called to Nolan's office to sign a letter confirming Cameron's false allegations. Todd reluctantly signs under his parents' pressure, and Keating is fired.
Nolan takes over Keating's English class. As Keating interrupts the class to gather his belongings, Todd confesses that the boys were pressured into signing the letter that led to his dismissal. Keating assures Todd that he believes him. Nolan threatens to expel Todd and anyone else who speaks out of line. Despite the threat, Todd stands up on his desk and says, "O Captain! My Captain!". Several other members of the Dead Poets Society, along with several classmates, follow suit. Touched by their support, Keating proudly thanks the boys and departs.

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Response
On review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, Dead Poets Society holds an approval rating of 85%, based on 66 reviews, with an average score of 7.2/10. The website's critical consensus reads: "Affecting performances from the young cast and a genuinely inspirational turn from Robin Williams grant Peter Weir's prep school drama top honors." On Metacritic, the film received a score of 79, based on 15 reviews, indicating "generally favorable" reviews. Audiences polled by CinemaScore gave the film a rare "A+" grade on a scale of A+ to F.
The Washington Post's reviewer called it "solid, smart entertainment", and praised Robin Williams for giving a "nicely restrained acting performance". Vincent Canby of The New York Times also praised Williams' "exceptionally fine performance", while writing that "Dead Poets Society... is far less about Keating than about a handful of impressionable boys."
Pauline Kael was unconvinced about the film and its "middlebrow highmindedness", but praised Williams. "Robin Williams' performance is more graceful than anything he's done before [–] he's totally, concentratedly there – [he] reads his lines stunningly, and when he mimics various actors reciting Shakespeare there's no undue clowning in it; he's a gifted teacher demonstrating his skills." Roger Ebert's review for the Chicago Sun-Times gave the film two stars out of four. He criticized Williams for spoiling an otherwise creditable dramatic performance by occasionally veering into his onstage comedian's persona, and lamented that for a film set in the 1950s, there was no mention of the Beat Generation writers popular among college students of the era. Additionally, Ebert described the film as an often poorly constructed "collection of pious platitudes... The movie pays lip service to qualities and values that, on the evidence of the screenplay itself, it is cheerfully willing to abandon."
On their Oscar-nomination edition of Siskel & Ebert, both Gene Siskel (who also gave the film a mixed review) and Ebert disagreed with Williams's Oscar nomination. Ebert said that he would have swapped Williams with either Matt Dillon for Drugstore Cowboy or John Cusack for Say Anything. On their If We Picked the Winners special in March 1990, Ebert chose the film's Best Picture nomination as the worst nomination of the year, believing that it took a slot that could have gone to Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing. Film historian Leonard Maltin wrote: "Well made, extremely well acted, but also dramatically obvious and melodramatically one-sided. Nevertheless, Tom Schulman's screenplay won an Oscar."
John Simon, writing for National Review, said that Dead Poets Society was the most dishonest film that he had seen in some time. Richard Schickel reviewed the film for Time, commenting: "Williams, who has comparatively little screen time, has come to act, not to cut comic riffs, and he does so with forceful, ultimately compelling, simplicity." Kevin Dettmar wrote in The Atlantic: "The beloved film's portrayal of studying literature is both misleading and deeply seductive." He commented further on how literature was taught in the film (by Robin Williams's character John Keating), describing it as "the literary equivalent of fandom," and "anti-intellectual".

## Reception > Legacy
After Robin Williams's death in August 2014, fans of his work used social media to pay tribute to him with photo and video reenactments of the film's final "O Captain! My Captain!" scene. Upon hearing about Williams's death, many teachers came forward to pay him their respects online and even revealed that they were inspired to become teachers because of his character, Mr. Keating, from Dead Poets Society.
Ethan Hawke and Josh Charles feature prominently in the music video for "Fortnight" by American singer Taylor Swift from her album The Tortured Poets Department (2024), as a nod to the similarity between the two titles.

## Reception > Lara Flynn Boyle Scenes
A majority of actress Lara Flynn Boyle's scenes were edited out of the final film despite her name being in the film's credits. Boyle went on a 1990 episode of Late Night with David Letterman saying she was totally edited out of the film. However, Boyle did appear in sections of the final film that showed the performance of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
